Crafted in 1957 for MGM's legendary General Manager Eddie Mannix, this Beverly Hills estate carries a cinematic lineage that has only been elevated over time. In 2010, the property underwent a meticulous reinvention - an almost complete rebuild that expanded the home from 5,000 to over 8,000 square feet - guided by a team of architects formerly with Pritzker Prize-winning David Chipperfield. Their influence is unmistakable in the restrained geometry, the Roman travertine detailing, and an intentional restraint that elevates simplicity into a statement. Clad entirely in reclaimed Montana oak, the facade sets the tone for interiors defined by natural materials, clean lines, and bespoke detailing. A private, gated drive leads to the entry gallery, setting up sight lines that capture Century City and ocean views on one end, and Downtown's skyline on the other. Enveloped by mature landscaping and sited on approx. 3/4 acres, this home feels like a rustic retreat while being moments from all the City has to offer. The main living area revolves around an open kitchen and a seamless indoor-outdoor flow created by pocketing glass doors that extend to the infinity pool, fire pit lounge, grassy yard, and a full outdoor entertaining sequence complete with bar, barbecue, and an expansive, shaded lower terrace. Inside, the west wing of the property offers two primary suites which each feature their own fireplaces, large dressing rooms, and spa-level baths with steam showers.  One additional bedroom suite completes the first level.  The second level offers an office, gym and  three additional bedrooms. Seven total baths, including two luxuriously-appointed powder rooms, continue the home's palette of oak, stone, and bronze. Additional amenities include a fully soundproofed theater designed with the warmth of a living room with adjacent bar and glass-enclosed wine display. Convenient Crestron automation runs throughout, and storage is abundant, including attic access from both the garage and the primary closet. Gallery spaces, excellent wall space for art, and adjustable art lighting reflect the eye of the current owner, a notable collector with works placed in institutions such as LACMA and Tate Modern. Positioned within one of Beverly Hills' most discreet and desirable pockets, north of Sunset Blvd., this estate pairs architectural intention with privacy, views, and a timeless material vocabulary - an understated yet commanding retreat above the city.

You may think you know San Bernardino. Then you arrive here. High above the valley, the city gives way to open hillsides, sweeping mountain views and a horizon that seems to go forever.

Built in 2020 and positioned along the ridgeline on an approximately 16,000-square-foot lot, this four-bedroom, three-bath home takes full advantage of its remarkable setting. From morning light across the mountains to the city glowing below after dark, the view isn't something you occasionally notice—it's part of the experience of living here.

Inside, the open-concept floor plan brings the living, dining and kitchen spaces together, creating an inviting setting for everyday living and entertaining. The kitchen is anchored by a large quartz-topped center island, stainless steel appliances and generous cabinetry. A large dedicated laundry room adds valuable storage and workspace.

Upstairs, the primary suite becomes its own escape with a soaking tub, dual vanities, walk-in closet and private balcony overlooking the surrounding hills and valley—a perfect place for morning coffee or a quiet end to the day.

And then there's the pool.

Set apart from the home and tucked higher into the hillside is an outdoor retreat that feels almost like discovering a second property. Follow the path up the ridge and you're greeted by a custom cocktail pool, gas fire bowls and a covered lounge area surrounded by sweeping views.

This isn't simply a pool in the backyard. It's a destination.

Spend an afternoon in the water, gather around the fire as the sun goes down, or settle beneath the covered patio as the lights begin appearing across the valley below. With open hillside surrounding the retreat and no home immediately behind it, the setting delivers a sense of separation that's increasingly difficult to find in Southern California.

And yet you're close to CSUSB, hiking and outdoor recreation, with convenient access to the 210 and 215 freeways.

Tattuplex, 2012. Tom Marble, Architect. Published in "Dwell," "Los Angeles Times" and appears in the Sixth Edition of Gebhard and Winters' "An Architectural Guidebook to Los Angeles," where it is described  as a "remote hillside shrine." The two-level duplex was conceived through an ongoing conversation between architect Tom Marble and owner Tim Tattu. Its custom prefab steel-frame and concrete structure follows a double-hexagon plan, creating a natural flow through an otherwise complex geometry. The initial plan was pushed and pulled through multiple studies, reaching its final form 95 variations later. The result is a building that feels deeply rooted to its site. Rooms open onto terraces and wide, framed views of the surrounding landscape, while shifts in level create a sense of discovery throughout the house. That same attention extends to the interior. Much of the furniture is integral to the architecture: custom Douglas fir cabinetry, shelving, desks and storage were designed specifically for the house and its geometry. A sculptural dining table by Vincent Pocsik sits naturally within this language of custom furnishings. Artwork by Pae White, artist and partner of Tom Marble, adds another layer to a house shaped from its inception by architecture, art and design. In 2016, Tattuplex was awarded the best Small Multi-Family Residential Building Award by the AIA.  Initially designed to function as a multi-family residence, it can also function as a single-family compound depending on need. Nearly every major room opens to a view of the Silver Lake reservoir and the hills beyond. Many of the custom indoor and outdoor furnishings are being included with the sale.

Designed by the legendary Richard Neutra FAIA and widely recognized as "The Logar House" this cornerstone of architectural significance is archived in the Getty Research Institute, eligible for Los Angeles Historic Places designation, and highlighted in the esteemed Museum of Modern Art (MOMA) publication "The Architecture of Richard Neutra: From International Style to California Modern." This home not only exemplifies Neutra's innovative design philosophy but also cements its legacy as a vital piece of modern architectural heritage.Completed from 1950 to 1951, this residence was the former home of James F. and Olive Logar, and is possibly the last Neutra home in North SFV. Nestled on a 30,800 square foot lot, the property offers 2,032 square feet of luxurious living space with 3 bedrooms and 4 bathrooms.Inspired by Neutra's 1949 Time Magazine cover, the Logars commissioned Neutra to envision a home that would embody the modernist spirit. Olive Logar described it as "a beautiful little ship at anchor." The L-shaped design, constructed from white cement plaster and redwood, features an open-plan central wing that serves as a living, dining, and study area.Personal terraces extend from each bedroom and the living room, seamlessly integrating indoor and outdoor spaces. The carport, emerging from the house, creates the effect of layered planes along the faade, enhancing its visual appeal. Neutra's description of the home as having a "visually blended" sense of atmospheric continuity is evident as you journey from the entrance, through the home, and out to the expansive lawn. This design, while lacking direct mimetic continuity, is rich in coordinated architectural and landscape responses. The Logar House has captured the imagination of filmmakers and scholars alike, frequently requested for film shoots and academic study. Its historical and architectural significance is vividly portrayed in black in white by famed architectural photographer Julius Shulman in the Getty Research Institute archives. Own a piece of architectural history with The Logar Housean enduring symbol of modern design, innovation, and elegance. DO NOT DISTURB OCCUPANT.

Designed by architect Cary Gepner, this home is rooted with deep caissons in centuries of European tradition, all while embracing the wild romance of Topanga. Sweeping cross-canyon views entrance, sheltered by a roof sheathed in over 400 year old Provencal tiles. A rooftop deck captures panoramic vistas across Topanga's rolling mountains and endless skies. Stepping through a handcrafted mesquite door, the home reveals an interior alive with color, texture, and history. A tiled staircase ascends to a dramatic Great Room where soaring beamed ceilings and towering windows frame the mountains beyond. An antique Egyptian chandelier hangs overhead. Saltillo floors mingle with hand-painted tiles from India, Malibu, and Catalina, while massive 200 year old Manchurian doors with sliding timber bars open to a sheltering loggia near a dancing fountain. Lounge before the living room's carved marble fireplace, surrounded by doors leading to wrap-around decks. Thick plaster lime washed walls, antique sconces, and arched passages create rooms that feel collected over generations. Prepare pizza in the wood fired pizza oven, in a kitchen graced with deeply veined pink travertine counters and copper sinks, handcrafted cabinetry, an antique carved marble hood, and a wood-burning pizza oven, that evoke the warmth of a French farmhouse. Throughout the home, marble mosaic tile embedded "rugs" from Aleppo and Damascus add artistry and permanence underfoot. Walk through an enfilade of arched doorways to the primary suite, where a travertine-framed window captures cinematic views of the canyon. A fireplace, jetted soaking tub, hand-carved marble sinks, bronze fixtures, and a spacious walk in closet create a luxurious sanctuary. Upstairs, an antique Romeo and Juliet balcony window from India overlooks the Great Room, while a bright upper room serves as an office, studio, or guest hideaway. On the lower level a cozy den leads you to two spacious bedrooms, a large bath with a vintage clawfoot tub, a color drenched hallway lined in closets and built-in shelving, and a laundry room. Outside, gardens scented with citrus blossoms and chaparral unfold in every direction. Espaliered pear trees descended from renowned horticulturist F.C. Reimer share the grounds with blood oranges, limes, olives, pomegranates, grapes, redwoods, giant sycamores, oaks, jacarandas, Japanese maples, truffle trees, roses, and a whimsical chicken villa. Hidden paths and quiet garden retreats reveal another beautiful view at every turn. Set in the sweet climate of lower Fernwood, near the beach and the Westside, all the gifts of this storied canyon are close by, including lovely shops, galleries, yoga studios, parks, hiking and riding trails, restaurants, an outdoor theater, and excellent schools. A property of rare soul, this Topanga villa marries the patina of centuries, and the poetry of the canyon. A place where Provence meets California, where global artistry meets the wild chaparrel, and where every detail feels touched by time.
